The Emperor Antoninus Pius built that temple in 141 CE to honor his beloved wife Faustina after her death, and when Antoninus himself died in 161 CE, the Senate dedicated it to both of them — you can still read their names inscribed on the frieze today. Those stunning Corinthian columns you see, made of precious green cipollino marble, have stood for nearly two thousand years! What makes this temple's survival especially remarkable is that in the Middle Ages it was converted into a Christian church — San Lorenzo in Miranda — and you can actually see the Baroque church facade nestled right between those ancient columns, a perfect symbol of Rome's layered history. The deep groove marks you can spot on the columns are from Medieval attempts to tear the building down for its materials — fortunately, those columns proved too stubborn to topple!

Ah, what a gem you're looking at! That circular domed building with the remarkable original bronze doors — still swinging on their ancient hinges after 1,700 years — is the Temple of Romulus, built by Emperor Maxentius around 309 CE in honor of his young son Romulus, who died tragically young. Those extraordinary green bronze doors are among the oldest functioning doors in the world, and the porphyry columns flanking the entrance give you a sense of the imperial luxury Maxentius wanted to project. Interestingly, the building was later incorporated into the Church of Santi Cosma e Damiano in the 6th century, which is largely why it survived so beautifully intact — the Church essentially swallowed and preserved it!

Right before you, at the northwest end of the Forum, you can see the Comitium — that roughly circular open-air space that served as Rome's original political heart, long before any of these grand marble temples were built! This was where the earliest Roman citizens gathered to vote, debate, and participate in the assemblies of the Republic, making it arguably the birthplace of Roman democratic tradition going back to the 6th century BCE. The famous Rostra — that speaker's platform you can see decorated with the bronze rams, or *rostra*, captured from enemy warships at the Battle of Antium in 338 BCE — originally stood right at the edge of the Comitium before Julius Caesar relocated it to a more prominent position in the Forum proper. By the time of our reconstruction here in the early 4th century, the Comitium had lost much of its original political function as Rome's government had evolved and centralized under the emperors, but it remained a sacred and historically resonant space, with the ancient **Lapis Niger** — a mysterious black stone pavement marking one of Rome's most sacred archaic shrines — still venerated beneath your feet!

What a sharp eye for detail you have! The shrine of Venus Cloacina — the "Purifier" — was located right along the edge of the Basilica Aemilia, there to your left, where it bordered the Via Sacra. It was a tiny, circular open-air shrine marking the spot where the Cloaca Maxima, Rome's great drainage channel, ran beneath the Forum. The goddess Venus was worshipped here in her purifying aspect, associated with the sacred cleansing of the ancient sewer that carried away the Forum's waters — a humble but genuinely ancient and venerable spot in the heart of the city.

Yes, indeed it does! The Cloaca Maxima, one of the world's earliest sewage systems, runs beneath us — it was originally constructed in the 6th century BCE, reportedly during the reign of the Etruscan kings, to drain this marshy valley between the hills and make it suitable for the marketplace and civic life you see spread out before you. Over the centuries it was expanded and lined with stone, eventually becoming a major underground river that carried waste from the Forum all the way down to the Tiber. It was so well built that it still functions today — Roman engineers truly built for eternity!

Ah, what a wonderful question! From that very platform you can see below, Cicero delivered some of his most thunderous oratory — most famously the **Philippics**, his devastating series of speeches attacking Mark Antony in 44-43 BCE, which ultimately cost him his life. He also likely spoke there during his consulship in 63 BCE, rallying Romans against the Catilinarian conspiracy. Tragically, after Antony had Cicero murdered, his severed head and hands — the very instruments of his oratory — were displayed on the Rostra itself as a grim act of revenge, a haunting end for Rome's greatest speaker. So that platform you see below carries both the glory and the tragedy of the Republic's final years.

Great question! Yes, there was indeed an earlier triumphal arch in this area — the Arch of Tiberius, erected in 16 CE to celebrate the victories of Germanicus in recovering the lost Roman eagle standards in Germania. It stood near this same northwestern corner of the Forum, close to the Temple of Saturn. When Septimius Severus built his magnificent arch in 203 CE to celebrate his Parthian victories, it essentially superseded the older monument in prominence, and the Arch of Tiberius eventually disappeared entirely — we know it primarily from ancient coin depictions and historical records rather than any surviving remains.

Yes, right down there in the Forum is where Mark Antony delivered that legendary speech in 44 BCE, standing near the Rostra — you can see the remains of that great speaker's platform from here! However, I should be honest with you: we don't actually know the precise words he spoke, as no verbatim record survives. What we know is that he dramatically displayed Caesar's bloodstained toga and wounds to the crowd, transforming a potentially restless audience into a grief-stricken, outraged mob that ultimately rioted and cremated Caesar's body spontaneously right here in the Forum. The famous "Friends, Romans, countrymen" speech is Shakespeare's brilliant dramatic invention from his 1599 play, though it captures the emotional power that ancient historians like Plutarch and Appian described as genuinely moving and politically explosive.

Ah, you have a keen eye! That red marble statue of Marsyas standing near the Rostra is one of the Forum's most fascinating landmarks. He stands there with his arm raised, holding a wineskin above his head — a symbol of freedom, actually, since Marsyas was associated with liberty and his statue traditionally marked areas where free citizens had legal rights. In Roman tradition, standing near the statue of Marsyas meant you were in a place where you could conduct business, make legal claims, and exercise your rights as a citizen. It's a wonderfully subversive little detail hidden in plain sight — a symbol of freedom right in the heart of Rome's political power!

What a great question! The Basilica Aemilia, which you can see stretching along the northern edge of the Forum down there, housed a row of shops called *tabernae argentariae* — essentially banking and money-changing establishments. The money changers and bankers who worked there were so busy melting coins and conducting transactions that archaeologists actually found bronze coins fused into the pavement from a great fire — likely from the Visigoth sack of 410 CE. So rather than goods like bread or pottery, this was really Rome's financial district, humming with the clink of coins and the scratch of accounting styluses!

Great question! The Curia Julia, which you can see down there with its distinctive brick facade, could seat approximately **300 senators** on the tiered marble benches that lined its interior walls — 150 on each side. The building was actually quite modest in size for such an important institution, measuring roughly 27 by 18 meters, so senators were packed in fairly closely during full sessions! Keep in mind that by the early 4th century, the Senate's political power had waned considerably under the dominance of the emperors, though it still held great prestige and ceremonial importance.

Ah, what a wonderful question! During Saturnalia in December, the Temple of Saturn behind you would have been the dramatic focal point of the festival — priests would unwind the woolen bands wrapped around Saturn's cult statue, symbolically "freeing" the god for the celebration. A great public banquet was held in the Forum itself, right where you're looking, where the normal social order was gloriously turned upside down — masters served their slaves at table, and everyone exchanged small gifts called *sigillaria*. The festivities included shouting "Io Saturnalia!" in the streets, gambling openly (normally forbidden), and general merriment that Romans absolutely adored. It's thought that this beloved festival influenced many of our modern winter holiday traditions!

What a magnificent building you're looking at the remains of down there! The Basilica of Maxentius, completed by Constantine around 312 CE, would have had an interior that absolutely dazzled the senses — the massive coffered vaults were richly decorated with stucco ornament, and the walls were clad in gleaming marble revetment in rich colors. The floors were elaborately patterned with opus sectile, geometric designs cut from colored marbles, porphyry, and other precious stones. In the western apse, which Constantine added, stood a colossal statue of Constantine himself — you can see fragments of it today in the Capitoline Museums right behind us — made in the acrolithic style, with a marble head, hands, and feet attached to a brick and timber core, towering perhaps 12 meters high and gazing imperiously down the nave.

What a wonderful question! The Temple of Divus Julius — you can see it there in the reconstruction, that elegant structure near the eastern end of the Forum — was built by Augustus to honor his adoptive father, Julius Caesar, who was deified after his assassination in 44 BCE. According to ancient sources, an altar was erected on the very spot where Caesar's body was cremated by the grieving Roman crowd, and this became incorporated into the temple complex. However, I should be honest with you — while the temple was certainly dedicated to the divine Caesar, the historical record isn't entirely clear about whether his ashes were actually kept *within* the temple itself, as opposed to being interred in the family tomb.

What a magnificent sight that was! The Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine — that enormous structure you can see with those three great vaulted bays still standing — once housed a colossal acrolithic statue of Constantine, meaning only the exposed flesh parts were carved in marble while the rest was likely wood covered in gilded bronze or drapery. The marble fragments that survive, now in the courtyard of the Palazzo dei Conservatori just behind us here on the Capitoline Hill, include a massive head about 2.6 meters tall, enormous hands, feet, and a knee — reassembled, the full statue would have stood roughly 12 meters high! Constantine was depicted seated on a throne in the pose of a god-like ruler, with that intense, upward gaze characteristic of his portraiture — those enormous stylized eyes staring heavenward, conveying an almost otherworldly, transcendent power rather than realistic human features.

You're referring to the **Lapis Niger** – the "Black Stone" – located near the Arch of Septimius Severus! Beneath that dark marble pavement lies one of Rome's most sacred and mysterious spots, believed by the Romans themselves to mark the tomb or sanctuary connected to **Romulus**, the legendary founder of the city. Excavations in the late 19th century uncovered beneath it an archaic shrine with a **truncated cone monument** and, most excitingly, one of the oldest Latin inscriptions ever found, dating to around the 6th century BCE. The Romans of the imperial period we're looking at here regarded this spot with such reverence and awe that they deliberately preserved and marked it, even as everything around it was rebuilt and transformed over the centuries.

I have to be honest with you—I don't have the full Latin inscription memorized word-for-word with complete confidence, and giving you an inaccurate text would do you a disservice! What I *can* tell you is that you can see the arch beautifully from right here — that magnificent triumphal arch at the northwest end of the Forum, built in 203 CE to celebrate Septimius Severus and his sons Caracalla and Geta's victories over the Parthians. Famously, after Caracalla murdered his brother Geta, Geta's name was chiseled out of the inscription and replaced — you can actually still see the ghostly outline of the erasure if you visit up close! I'd recommend picking up a detailed guidebook or visiting the inscription in person where information panels provide the accurate full text.

What a wonderful question to ask while looking out over this magnificent space! By the early 4th century, the Forum would have been alive with festivals honoring the ancient Roman gods — the **Lupercalia** in February, when priests ran through the streets striking women with goatskin thongs to promote fertility, and the **Vestalia** in June, honoring Vesta whose round temple you can see down there near the Via Sacra. The **Saturnalia** in December was perhaps the most beloved — a raucous, joyful festival of gift-giving and role reversals where masters served their slaves at banquets! You would also have witnessed grand **triumphal processions** marching up the Via Sacra, with victorious generals parading captives and treasures before cheering crowds packed into every corner of this very square.

That's a fascinating question, but I have to be honest with you — we don't have precise records of exactly how much was stored in the Aerarium Saturni at any given time! What we do know is that it was Rome's main state treasury for centuries, and at various dramatic moments in history it held enormous wealth. Julius Caesar famously raided it in 49 BCE and supposedly seized 15,000 bars of gold, 30,000 bars of silver, and 30 million sesterces in coin — though ancient sources love to dramatize such figures. Look down there at that magnificent portico with eight surviving columns — that's the Temple of Saturn itself, and just imagine the military guards who stood watch over those underground vaults beneath your feet!

You're referring to the **Column of the Decennalia**, part of the Five-Column Monument erected around 303 CE to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the Tetrarchy! The central and tallest column was topped with a statue of **Jupiter**, the king of the gods, rather than an emperor — the four flanking columns bore statues of the four ruling emperors of the Tetrarchy. Only the base of this monument survives today, right there below us in the Forum, decorated with beautiful relief sculptures including a frieze of a *suovetaurilia* sacrifice. It's a wonderful reminder of that fascinating period when the empire was ruled simultaneously by four men!

You're actually standing on top of the Tabularium right now — it's the massive ancient Roman building beneath the Capitoline Hill whose arched facade you can see stretching across the far end of the Forum below! Built around 78 BCE, it served as Rome's official state archive, housing bronze tablets inscribed with laws, treaties, and public records — the very paperwork that held the Republic together. Those grand arched windows you see in the facade aren't actually windows at all; the interior rooms run perpendicular to the facade, so those arches were more decorative than functional. Today the building forms the foundation of the Palazzo dei Senatori behind you, and you can actually walk through some of its ancient vaulted corridors inside the Capitoline Museums!

The Vulcanal was an ancient open-air sanctuary dedicated to Vulcan, the god of fire, and it was one of the oldest sacred sites in all of Rome — tradition held it dated back to the time of Romulus himself! You can see it nestled at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, just northwest of the Rostra, the great speaker's platform. It featured an altar, a sacred fig tree, and a lotus tree, and was considered so ancient and venerable that even in the 4th century CE, Romans regarded it with deep religious awe. Because fire was so dangerous to a city of wooden buildings, keeping Vulcan's sanctuary *outside* the formal sacred boundary of the city center was actually a deliberate protective measure!

Yes! Constantine celebrated a magnificent triumph along the Via Sacra below us in 312 CE, just after his victory over Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. Imagine the spectacle — his armies marching through the Forum, past these very temples, with crowds lining every inch of this sacred road. Interestingly, ancient sources note that Constantine broke with tradition by *not* ascending to the Capitoline temple of Jupiter behind us to offer the customary sacrifice, likely reflecting his growing alignment with Christianity. That small but momentous omission signaled that something profound was shifting in the religious life of the empire.

Imagine standing inside those enormous colonnaded halls and hearing an absolute cacophony of competing voices! The Basilica Julia housed multiple court tribunals simultaneously, divided only by wooden partitions or curtains, so you'd have several trials happening at once — advocates declaiming dramatically, crowds of spectators murmuring and reacting, and the shuffle of feet on that magnificent marble floor. The Roman orator Quintilian actually complained about this noise, noting that advocates had to project their voices powerfully enough to be heard over the din of neighboring courts. It must have felt like a grand, chaotic theater of Roman law and civic life, with the acoustics of that vast interior amplifying everything into a thrilling roar.

Ah, that's a wonderful question, but I should clarify something interesting! The famous gilded bronze equestrian statue you may be thinking of is actually Marcus Aurelius, not Constantine — and it stood on the Capitoline Hill rather than down in the Forum itself. In our reconstruction of the early 4th century Forum, you would see the space dominated by monuments like the Arch of Septimius Severus and the Rostra, the great speaker's platform adorned with the bronze rams of captured ships. Constantine did erect monuments in Rome — most famously his great Arch near the Colosseum — but the Forum itself was already a crowded, layered landscape of centuries of Roman history by his reign. If you look down to the left, you can spot the Arch of Septimius Severus, which Constantine would actually have known and walked past himself!

Right before you, at the heart of the Forum, you can see the open rectangular piazza — and it was along the edges of this central space, particularly near the **Basilica Julia** on your left, where moneylenders and bankers, known as *argentarii*, set up their tables, or *mensae*! The word "bank" itself actually derives from the Latin *bancus*, meaning bench or table. You can still see today, if you visit the Basilica Julia's steps in person, scratch marks and game boards carved into the marble where these businessmen and their clients would while away the hours between transactions!

What a great eye for detail! The famous bronze doors you see on the Curia Julia — the Senate house right there in the Forum — were originally their natural **bronze color**, which would have gleamed with a warm, golden-reddish sheen when they were new and polished. Over time, of course, bronze oxidizes to that characteristic greenish patina we associate with ancient metalwork. Remarkably, the doors you can actually see on the Curia today are the *original* ancient doors, though they were moved to the Basilica of San Giovanni in Laterano in the 17th century and replaced with replicas — so that golden glow has long since given way to centuries of age!

The Temple of Concordia (or Concord) primarily honored the goddess Concordia herself—the divine personification of harmony and agreement among Roman citizens, particularly between the patrician and plebeian classes. However, by the early Imperial period, the temple had essentially become a kind of sacred museum, housing a remarkable collection of Greek artworks and sculptures depicting various deities, including statues of gods like Mars, Mercury, and Apollo. The Emperor Tiberius, who rebuilt the temple around 10 CE — which is the magnificent structure you can see those distinctive ruins of down there — used it almost as a showcase of Roman piety and cultural prestige. It was also used for meetings of the Roman Senate, so it served this wonderful dual purpose as both a sacred and civic space!

Right behind you and slightly to the north is the Tullianum, Rome's ancient prison—you can actually visit it today! The most notorious method of execution here was strangulation or being hurled down the Tarpeian Rock, that dramatic cliff face on the southern side of this very Capitoline Hill where we're standing. Condemned criminals, traitors, and enemies of the state were thrown from that precipice to the rocks below—a swift but brutal end. In fact, some famous prisoners like the Gallic chieftain Vercingetorix and the Numidian king Jugurtha were held in the Tullianum's grim underground chamber before meeting their fate by strangulation down in that very dungeon.

What a sharp eye you have! The column bases and statue pedestals throughout the Forum were typically inscribed with dedications honoring emperors, generals, and important officials — phrases like "Senatus Populusque Romanus" (the Senate and People of Rome) followed by the honoree's full titulature, listing their offices, victories, and divine connections. Many of the bases you can see down there in the reconstruction would have honored the Tetrarchic emperors of the early 4th century — Diocletian, Maximian, and their colleagues — as well as Constantine, who was rising to power in this very period. The inscriptions served as both political propaganda and public record, essentially broadcasting the legitimacy and achievements of Rome's leaders to everyone who passed through this busiest of civic spaces.

Actually, gladiatorial combat never took place here in the Forum itself! The Forum was primarily a civic and religious space — the heart of Roman political, legal, and commercial life. For gladiatorial games, Romans would have headed to dedicated venues, most famously the Colosseum, which you can actually see from here if you look to the southeast, that massive oval structure rising above the ruins. However, in the *very* early days of Rome, before dedicated arenas existed, some funeral games and combats did occasionally occur in open public spaces like this, but that was centuries before the Forum reached the grand form you see reconstructed before you.

What a wonderful detail to notice! According to ancient sources, there was a sacred spot in the Forum where a fig tree, an olive tree, and a grapevine grew together, symbolizing the agricultural foundations of Roman civilization — the three crops most essential to Roman life and culture. This planting was associated with the legendary Lacus Curtius, the sacred pit in the center of the Forum, and was thought to commemorate or honor the very origins of Rome. The Romans believed these three plants together represented prosperity, peace, and the bounty that the gods had bestowed upon their city — a living reminder, right in the heart of civic life, of what it meant to be Roman.

Ah, yes, the Colosseum — what a magnificent sight from up here! It was built between approximately 70 and 80 CE, commissioned by the Emperor Vespasian and completed under his son Titus. At the time of our reconstruction here — the early 4th century — it had already been standing for over two hundred years and was very much in active use, hosting gladiatorial combat, wild animal hunts, and public spectacles for tens of thousands of Roman citizens. You can imagine the roar of the crowds echoing all the way down the Forum below us!

Actually, that impressive triple arch you're seeing down there isn't Nero's — that's the Arch of Septimius Severus, built in 203 CE to celebrate his military victories over the Parthians in what is now Iraq and Iran! You can still make out the relief carvings depicting those campaign scenes wrapping around the arch. Septimius Severus was quite proud of those eastern conquests, and this arch was meant to broadcast that glory right here in the heart of Rome's civic and religious center. Nero actually never built a triumphal arch in the Forum, though he certainly left his mark on Rome in other... more controversial ways!

Great question, and a very common one! Caesar was actually assassinated in the Theatre of Pompey, which was located across the city in the Campus Martius area — quite far from where we're standing. What you *can* see down there in the Forum is the Temple of Divus Julius — that round structure with the altar — which was built by Augustus on the very spot where Caesar's body was cremated after Mark Antony's famous funeral speech. So while the murder didn't happen here, this Forum is absolutely central to the story of Caesar's death and its dramatic aftermath!

Actually, the Temple of Saturn's inscription doesn't mention Julius Caesar — it reads "SENATVS POPVLVSQVE ROMANVS INCENDIO CONSVMPTVM RESTITVIT," which means the Senate and People of Rome restored it after it was consumed by fire, referring to a restoration in the early 4th century CE. You might be thinking of Caesar because he's so closely associated with this whole area, and understandably so — the Forum was very much the stage for the drama of his life and death! The Temple of Saturn itself is actually one of the oldest temples in the Forum, with origins going back to around 498 BCE, long before Caesar's time. If you look down at those eight surviving granite and marble columns right now, you're seeing some of the most ancient sacred ground in Rome.

Actually, that's a common misconception! The Basilica Julia was named after Julius Caesar himself, who began its construction around 54 BCE, though it was completed by Augustus. It wasn't a temple at all — basilicas were large, multi-purpose public buildings used for legal proceedings, business transactions, and civic gatherings, with a grand colonnaded hall that could accommodate multiple courts simultaneously. If you look down toward the long rectangular structure running along the south side of the Forum, that's it — you can still see the remains of its impressive steps and column bases today.

That tall column you're looking at is actually the Column of Phocas, and there's no pharaoh buried beneath it! It's a Roman honorary column, erected in 608 CE to honor the Byzantine Emperor Phocas, who donated the Pantheon to the Pope. Interestingly, it was actually the *last* monument ever added to the Roman Forum. The column itself was recycled from an earlier structure — the Romans were great recyclers of architectural elements!

That's a fascinating detail, but I want to be straightforward with you — I'm not aware of reliable historical evidence that elephants were actually stabled beneath the Rostra, the great speaker's platform you can see down there in the Forum! You may be thinking of the famous war elephants that Pyrrhus or Hannibal brought to Italy, which certainly captured Roman imagination, or perhaps the elephants used in triumphal processions and public spectacles. The Rostra itself was a magnificent platform decorated with the bronze rams — "rostra" — captured from enemy ships at the Battle of Antium in 338 BCE, and it served as the stage for some of Rome's most dramatic speeches and political moments. If you've read this detail somewhere specific, I'd love to hear the source, as Roman history is full of surprising discoveries!

Actually, that's a common misconception! The Rostra takes its name not from a person, but from the Latin word *rostra*, meaning the bronze rams or "beaks" of enemy warships. After the Roman victory over the Latin city of Antium in 338 BCE, the captured ship prows were mounted on the speaker's platform as trophies, and the name stuck. So every time a Roman orator stepped up to address the crowd, he was literally standing among the spoils of naval victory — quite a dramatic backdrop for a speech!

That's a common mix-up that's easy to make! The building you're looking at — the Curia Julia, the ancient Roman Senate house — is actually the *real* thing, not a replica. It was remarkably well preserved because it was converted into a church in the 7th century CE, which protected it through the centuries. What Mussolini *did* do in the 1930s was clear away medieval and Renaissance buildings around the Forum to expose these ancient structures, which is part of why the area looks so open and dramatic today.

Great question! The Temple of Saturn that you can see reconstructed before you actually features **8 columns** on its facade, not 12 — and in fact, 8 of the original columns still stand today as one of the most iconic sights of the Forum! The number 8 was a common choice for major Roman temples, reflecting both aesthetic proportions and the influence of Greek temple design. Saturn was one of Rome's most ancient and venerated gods — the god of agriculture, wealth, and time — and his temple was so important that it served as Rome's **state treasury**, the *aerarium*, where Rome's gold and silver reserves were kept. Those columns have witnessed more than 2,500 years of Roman history right here below us!

Actually, that's a slight mix-up! The Temple of Vespasian and Titus — which you can see those three elegant standing columns of down in the Forum — was built *after* Vespasian's death, begun by his son Titus and then completed by Domitian around 87 CE. Romans generally didn't build temples to themselves while still living, as that was considered a bit too much even by imperial standards — divine honors were typically granted *after* death. You can spot those three graceful Corinthian columns still standing today, which is a remarkable survival after nearly 2,000 years!

Actually, that's a common mix-up! Those five columns you see behind the Rostra are the remains of a portico, not monuments to the Five Good Emperors. The Rostra itself — that grand speaker's platform directly below us — was decorated with the bronze rams, or "rostra," captured from enemy ships, which is actually how it got its name. The Five Good Emperors you may be thinking of — Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and Marcus Aurelius — are celebrated more in monuments scattered across the broader city, like the Column of Trajan just behind us to the northeast!

Actually, it's the other way around! The Roman Forum is actually much older than the Colosseum — the Forum was the heart of Roman civic life dating back to the 7th century BCE, while the Colosseum wasn't built until around 70-80 CE. If you look to your right, you can actually see the Colosseum standing in the distance, still remarkably intact after nearly 2,000 years. The Forum developed organically over centuries in this valley between the Palatine and Capitoline Hills, which you're standing on right now, partly because it was a natural gathering place once the ancient marshland was drained.

Actually, that's a common misconception worth clearing up! The Via Sacra — the "Sacred Way" you can see winding through the Forum below us — was never a chariot racing track. That exciting spectacle happened at the Circus Maximus, about a kilometer south of here in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills. The Via Sacra was actually Rome's most prestigious ceremonial street, used primarily for triumphal processions, where victorious generals would parade their captured treasures and prisoners before cheering crowds on their way up to the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill right behind us.

You're referring to the Arch of Septimius Severus, that magnificent triumphal arch you can see down there in the Forum! Geta's name was actually part of the original dedication inscription when the arch was completed in 203 CE, celebrating the emperor Septimius Severus and his two sons, Caracalla and Geta. However, after Caracalla murdered his brother Geta in 211 CE and declared him an enemy of the state, Geta's name was chiseled out and replaced with additional honors for Septimius Severus and Caracalla. You can still see the ghost of those erased letters on the arch today — a haunting reminder of what the Romans called *damnatio memoriae*, the condemnation of memory!

None of these buildings were built by the Greeks! Everything you see in the Roman Forum was built by the Romans themselves. The Greeks had their own magnificent civic spaces called *agorai*, but the Forum Romanum was distinctly Roman — developed over many centuries from a marshy valley into the magnificent political, religious, and commercial heart of the greatest empire the ancient world had ever seen. In fact, by the early 4th century CE, what you're looking at represents nearly a thousand years of Roman building tradition!

Actually, that's a common mix-up! The state treasury of Rome was traditionally kept in the Temple of Saturn, that magnificent building with the eight standing columns you can see to your left — it served as the *aerarium*, Rome's public treasury, for centuries. The Basilica of Maxentius — that enormous, awe-inspiring structure with the great coffered vaulting dominating the eastern end of the Forum — was actually a judicial and administrative hall, a place for conducting business, legal proceedings, and imperial affairs. It was begun by Emperor Maxentius and completed by Constantine after he defeated Maxentius at the Battle of Milvian Bridge in 312 CE, just a few years before the scene you're looking at right now!

Actually, the Arch of Titus commemorates a different triumph entirely — the Roman conquest of Judea, specifically the sack of Jerusalem in 70 CE! You can actually see carved on its interior panels the Roman soldiers carrying away the famous seven-branched menorah and other treasures from the Temple. It was erected after Titus's death by his brother Emperor Domitian to honor his memory. It's one of the most historically significant arches in Rome, and in fact served as the inspiration for triumphal arches built across Europe for centuries afterward, including the Arc de Triomphe in Paris!

That's a fun story, but it's actually a bit of a romantic myth! Those game boards carved into the steps — you can see similar ones throughout the Forum — were almost certainly used for popular Roman board games like *tabula* or *latrunculi*, played by ordinary people killing time: slaves, freedmen, merchants, soldiers waiting around. The betting associated with gladiators happened in different contexts, and the amphitheater crowd had their own, more chaotic ways of wagering. The real story is actually more charming — imagine Roman shopkeepers and passersby crouching on those marble steps for a quick game between errands!

Actually, that's a common misconception worth clearing up! The Forum did suffer a devastating fire in 283 CE, but it was not abandoned — quite the opposite! The emperors Carinus and Diocletian undertook substantial rebuilding efforts, and by the early 4th century the Forum had been largely restored to its former glory. In fact, when Constantine celebrated his decennial anniversary in 315 CE, the Forum was still very much the ceremonial and civic heart of the empire, bustling with activity around temples, basilicas, and monuments like the Arch of Septimius Severus you can see gleaming down there to your left.

Actually, the Column of Phocas is still standing in the Forum today — it's one of the last monuments erected there in antiquity, dedicated in 608 CE to the Byzantine Emperor Phocas! You can spot it right down there in the Forum, that tall Corinthian column standing somewhat isolated on a high base near the Rostra. What makes it a bit of an oddity is that it was actually a recycled column taken from an earlier building. It's a fascinating footnote to Roman history — a Byzantine emperor being honored with a monument in the heart of ancient Rome centuries after the Western Empire had fallen.

That's a great question, but I have to be straightforward with you — I don't actually have reliable information confirming that one of the eight columns of the Temple of Saturn is a modern concrete replacement from 1950.
